stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Musicologist Ines Arroyo traces one of the stranger reversals in the history of Western dance music. The chaconne—imported to Spain from the Americas around 1600, sung with bawdy refrains, and condemned by clerics, who tried to ban it from Madrid's theaters ______ within a century, slowed into the solemn variation form that Bach would later use in his Partita in D minor.
explanation: The interruption that describes the chaconne opens with a dash right after "The chaconne," so it has to close with a dash too. Remove everything between the dashes and you get "The chaconne was, within a century, slowed into the solemn variation form..." That is a complete sentence. The comma inside the phrase, before "who," opens the relative clause, and that clause ends where the dash interruption ends. The closing dash therefore finishes both at once, and the main verb "was" follows with no conjunction.

B.why: You saw the comma before "who" and closed the most recent element with a matching comma, so you lost track of the dash that opened the interruption much earlier. The dash is never closed, which leaves an interruption opened with a dash and closed with a comma. The marks at the two ends of an interruption must match.

C.why: A semicolon needs a complete sentence on each side. "The chaconne—imported ... theaters" has no main verb, and "was, within a century, slowed..." has no subject, so both sides are fragments.

D.why: You closed the dash correctly, but then you added "and," which treats the sentence as if it joins two things. Nothing comes before "was" for "and" to join it to: "The chaconne" has no earlier main verb. Removing the interruption leaves "The chaconne and was slowed...," which is not grammatical.

subtype_name: Close the interrupter: match the opening comma

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Immunologists long assumed that the adult immune system could do without its earliest training ground. The thymus, an organ that, in most people, reaches its greatest size at puberty and is then slowly replaced by fat ______ to produce small numbers of new T cells well into middle age, according to a 2024 imaging study of 300 volunteers.
explanation: The appositive "an organ that ... replaced by fat" opens with the comma after "The thymus" and has to close with a comma after "fat." Leave the commas around "in most people" alone, because they belong to a smaller interruption inside the appositive. The word "however" then gets its own pair of commas. Cross out both interruptions and you get "The thymus continues to produce small numbers of new T cells..." That is a complete sentence, with "thymus" as the subject and "continues" as its verb.

B.why: You saw "however" and automatically put a semicolon before it. Adding "it" makes the text after the semicolon a complete sentence, so that side passes the test. The text before it does not: "The thymus, an organ that ... replaced by fat" has no main verb. A semicolon cannot follow a fragment.

C.why: You left the appositive unclosed. It opened with a comma after "The thymus," so it needs a matching comma after "fat." Without that comma, "however" runs into the appositive and the sentence never clearly returns to its subject.

D.why: You added "and," which makes "continues" read as a second verb joined to "reaches" and "is replaced" inside the appositive. The subject "The thymus" is then left with no main verb, and the appositive never gets its closing comma.
